title: Replace a live table without an empty-name gap
goal: Publish a complete replacement atomically while preserving the product-specific identity, history, and access behavior you actually need.
tag: Focused certification lesson · table deployment and recovery · cycle 4, position 3
concept:
A grocery shelf should switch from yesterday's price list to today's complete list in one move. Taking the old list down and building the new one line by line leaves shoppers with an empty or half-built list.

An atomic replacement makes one catalog decision: readers see the old complete table or the new complete table, never the gap between DROP and CREATE. Databricks replaces the contents while keeping the table identity and Delta history. Snowflake can swap the names of two prepared table objects in one transaction. Those are related outcomes, not the same mechanism.
example: prod.orders has 3 validated rows. A rebuild creates 4 corrected rows. With drop-then-create, a reader between statements sees “table missing.” With Databricks CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE, the named table moves from version 7 to version 8. With Snowflake ALTER TABLE prod.orders SWAP WITH prod.orders_next, the two table names exchange objects atomically.

use_case.when: Use atomic replacement when a full snapshot or corrected rebuild must become visible to concurrent readers as one publication event.
use_case.example: A nightly customer dimension rebuild must publish 40 million validated rows without exposing an empty table to dashboards.
use_case.decision: Use incremental MERGE when only a small known delta changes. Use replacement when the entire result is authoritative, validation happens before publication, rollback is planned, and product-specific grants, policies, streams, dependencies, and history have been checked.

practice: Choose drop/create or atomic publication. Step through a reader arriving before, during, and after the switch; then inspect the distinct Databricks and Snowflake identity paths.
boundary: The local model has two snapshots and three reader moments. It does not execute either product, model concurrent writers, streaming checkpoints, streams, dynamic tables, foreign dependencies, grants, policies, retention, storage costs, or every DDL restriction. Vendor SQL was not run.

product_sections.title: Databricks: replace contents, keep the table identity
product_sections.html:
The same shelf gets a new complete edition. For Delta tables, CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE is one transaction. Databricks documents that the table identity and history remain, concurrent readers can continue, granted privileges are preserved, and matching column masks remain. A drop followed by create does not have those semantics.

-- sourced SQL sketch; not executedCREATE OR REPLACE TABLE prod.orders ASSELECT * FROM stage.orders_validated;-- rollback evidence: DESCRIBE HISTORY prod.orders;

Failure/fix. Drop/recreate breaks the active name-to-history link and can surprise concurrent work. Prefer replace for a supported Delta replacement, but verify schema, masks, row filters, dependencies, protocol/runtime constraints, and concurrent-write behavior.

Execution label. SQL is an unexecuted vendor sketch. The identity/version diagram is local JavaScript.

product_sections.title: Snowflake: prepare blue and green objects, then swap their names
product_sections.html:
Two carts exchange shelf labels. Build and validate ORDERS_NEXT. ALTER TABLE ORDERS SWAP WITH ORDERS_NEXT renames the two table objects in one transaction. Afterward, the production name points to the prepared object and the previous production object remains under the other name for inspection or rollback.

-- sourced SQL sketch; not executedCREATE TABLE PROD.ORDERS_NEXT CLONE PROD.ORDERS;-- rebuild and validate ORDERS_NEXTALTER TABLE PROD.ORDERS SWAP WITH PROD.ORDERS_NEXT;

Failure/fix. A swap needs ownership on both tables plus the documented schema privilege, and temporary/permanent combinations have restrictions. Names move between objects; inspect grants, policies, streams, dependencies, retention, and rollback behavior rather than assuming Databricks-style identity preservation.

title: Cancelled scheduled tasks can stay in the queue for hours
goal: Remove cancelled delayed tasks promptly when retaining them would turn churn into a memory problem.
concept:
Canceling a hotel reservation should free the room card from the front desk's future-arrivals tray. A crossed-out card left there for six months still occupies space.

By default, a cancelled task in ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor can remain in its work queue until its delay elapses. The task will not run, but its queue node—and objects reachable from it—can remain retained. setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true) removes a task from the queue when cancellation succeeds.
example: A service schedules three one-hour retry timers, then cancels all three when the request completes. Default policy: queue size remains 3. Remove-on-cancel policy: queue size becomes 0 immediately.

use_case.when: Enable prompt removal when a long-lived scheduler creates and cancels many long-delay tasks, and retention is more costly than post-cancel inspection.
use_case.example: Each API request schedules a 24-hour expiry task but usually cancels it after a two-second successful response.
use_case.decision: Measure cancellation churn and retained heap first. If delayed tasks are few or inspection matters, the default may be acceptable. Also bound captured task state; policy does not make an unbounded live schedule safe.

practice: Change the number of one-hour timers and cancel them. Compare the queue under the default and remove-on-cancel policies.
boundary: The Java replay uses three tasks with one-hour delays and inspects queue size immediately. It does not measure retained bytes, GC roots, race timing, executor shutdown policies, periodic tasks, production throughput, or every JDK implementation.

title: When overloaded, finish valuable work before starting expendable work
goal: Use explicit admission priority and cheap rejection to preserve useful completions instead of letting every request time out.
concept:
A crowded emergency room does not start every case and leave all patients half-treated. It admits work it can finish and gives scarce capacity to the outcomes that matter most.

Under overload, accepting everything creates queues, timeouts, retries, and more load. Load shedding rejects excess work early. Priority makes the rejection policy explicit: health checks and completion calls can outrank new optional work. Measure successful-request latency and useful completions—goodput—separately from fast rejections.
example: A service can finish 100 cost units per second. It receives 80 checkout-completion units and 50 crawler units. FIFO after crawler traffic arrived first admits 50 crawler and only 50 checkout. Priority admission finishes all 80 checkout and admits 20 crawler; 30 crawler units are rejected early.

use_case.when: Use load shedding after defining measured capacity, bounded queues, client retry behavior, and business-visible priorities.
use_case.example: During an Availability Zone impairment, preserve payment completion and health checks while shedding recommendation refreshes and crawlers.
use_case.decision: Add capacity and fix bottlenecks for sustained legitimate load. Shed only excess work during brownout, make rejection cheap, communicate retry semantics, test beyond the goodput plateau, and ensure shedding does not hide the autoscaling signal.

practice: Change capacity and workload mix. Compare FIFO admission with priority admission and watch completed checkout work, rejected work, and wasted queue pressure.
boundary: This arithmetic model treats every unit as equal cost within a class and has one server interval. It does not model latency distributions, fairness, retries, dependency priorities, queue age, health checks, autoscaling, AZ loss, or real customer value.

title: Use an agent as a tool when one manager must keep the conversation
goal: Choose manager-style delegation or handoff based on who must own the next turn and the shared conversation state.
concept:
A restaurant host can ask the chef a question and return with the answer, or escort the guest to the chef and leave them together. Both involve a specialist; only one changes who owns the conversation.

With agents as tools, a manager invokes specialists and stays responsible for synthesis and user interaction. With a handoff, the selected specialist becomes the active agent and receives the conversation history. In the OpenAI Agents SDK, a nested tool-agent run does not automatically inherit the parent's conversation state; share an explicit session or continuation strategy only when that is intended.
example: An incident manager asks a Kafka specialist for lag diagnosis and a Snowflake specialist for warehouse evidence, then returns one combined plan. That is manager style. A support triage agent that transfers a refund conversation to a refund specialist uses a handoff.

use_case.when: Use manager style when one agent must enforce policy, combine several specialist results, or preserve a single user-facing voice. Use a handoff when one specialist should own subsequent turns.
use_case.example: A platform-incident agent calls Spark and Kafka agents as tools, redacts their outputs, then makes one rollback recommendation.
use_case.decision: Start with one agent and ordinary tools. Add specialists only when instructions or evaluation evidence justify separation. Decide explicitly whether history, application context, approvals, sessions, and tracing cross the boundary.

practice: Switch between manager and handoff. Add a second specialist request and watch whether one manager can synthesize both or control moves to one peer.
boundary: The browser model only tracks control ownership and visible messages. It does not run the SDK, a model, tools, sessions, tracing, approvals, retries, token budgets, or security policy. The Python trace is an executed teaching model, not an agent run.

title: A tailored molecule can connect one long-lived spin to one photon
goal: Understand what the reported single-molecule spin–photon interface demonstrated and what quantum-network engineering still requires.
concept:
A network needs a stable memory that can also speak through light. The spin stores quantum information; a photon can carry it to another node.

Researchers embedded a triplet ground-state carbene molecule in a structurally matched host crystal and addressed individual molecules. They report narrow zero-phonon optical lines, spectral stability beyond an hour, spin-selective optical transitions, single-molecule optical magnetic-resonance readout, millisecond-scale dynamical-decoupling coherence, and tens-of-milliseconds spin relaxation at 4.5 K.
example: The interactive teaching model gives a candidate link four gates: single-molecule optical addressability, stable narrow emission, spin-selective transitions, and useful spin coherence. Removing any gate breaks that toy link. The paper supplies evidence for these properties in its system; the model does not calculate network fidelity.

use_case.when: Use this result when evaluating molecular platforms for quantum networking, distributed quantum information, or chemically tunable single-emitter research.
use_case.example: A research group wants bottom-up chemical control of a node that combines optical access with a longer-lived spin state.
use_case.decision: Treat it as a platform demonstration, not a deployable quantum repeater. Compare collection efficiency, indistinguishability, entanglement fidelity/rate, cryogenic requirements, fabrication yield, integration, and lifetime before selecting an architecture.

practice: Toggle the four interface gates. Predict whether the toy node can store, address, and optically connect before revealing the link status.
boundary: The Boolean teaching model does not reproduce the experiment, spectra, Hamiltonian, ODMR, coherence fits, photon indistinguishability, entanglement, collection efficiency, fabrication yield, or network rate. Claims are limited to the primary paper, and practical quantum networking remains research.

title: A workflow_run privilege jump must treat build artifacts as hostile input
goal: Separate untrusted tests from privileged publication without turning the artifact bridge into code execution.
concept:
A loading dock may accept a sealed package from outside. The badge that opens the vault must not execute instructions found inside that package.

A workflow triggered by workflow_run can have secrets and write tokens even when the earlier workflow did not. That makes it useful for privilege separation—and dangerous if it checks out untrusted code or executes an artifact from the untrusted run. The privileged workflow must verify the originating run and treat downloaded files as data.
example: A fork pull request runs tests with read-only permissions and uploads result.json. The privileged follow-up checks the triggering workflow name, successful conclusion, head repository and SHA, downloads the expected artifact, validates its digest/schema, and posts a comment. It never runs a script from the archive.

use_case.when: Use workflow_run when an unprivileged build must be followed by a narrowly privileged action such as commenting, labeling, or publication.
use_case.example: Fork PR tests produce a JSON coverage summary; a later workflow with pull-request write permission posts the number.
use_case.decision: Keep the privileged follow-up tiny. Prefer passing identifiers or strict data. If the second workflow must execute build output, redesign the boundary or rebuild trusted code from a verified commit; do not rely on an artifact filename alone.

practice: Toggle origin verification, artifact validation, and artifact execution. Watch the privilege bridge remain data-only or become a repository compromise path.
boundary: The model simplifies GitHub events, permissions, artifact APIs, attestations, branch filters, forks, caches, reusable workflows, and token scopes. It does not execute Actions or prove a workflow secure.

title: A gRPC status code says the class; typed details say what the client may do
goal: Return machine-readable error details without turning human message text into retry or remediation logic.
concept:
A road sign says “closed.” A second sign says “reopens in 30 minutes” and a third names the blocked lane. The first classifies the problem; the details guide a safe response.

Every gRPC client can read a standard status code and message. With Protocol Buffers, the richer error model can attach typed detail messages in trailing metadata—for example RetryInfo, BadRequest, or QuotaFailure. Clients branch on code and known detail types, not on unstable English text.
example: A warehouse API returns RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, message “tenant burst quota exceeded,” RetryInfo{retry_delay:30s}, and QuotaFailure{subject:tenant/42}. A client that owns an idempotent request may schedule one retry after 30 seconds. A client that does not understand the details still sees the standard code.

use_case.when: Use typed details when clients need structured remediation such as field violations, retry delay, resource identity, quota subject, or support links.
use_case.example: A cross-language ingestion client needs to distinguish malformed rows from a temporary tenant quota and show the exact invalid fields.
use_case.decision: Keep the canonical code stable and details small. Add rich details only when target language libraries and intermediaries preserve them. Do not expose stack traces or sensitive resource data, and do not tell clients to retry non-idempotent operations blindly.

practice: Change the status code, retry detail, and request idempotency. Watch the client choose retry, fix-input, or stop without parsing the message string.
boundary: The local model is a dictionary decision table, not gRPC or protobuf encoding. It omits HTTP/2 trailers, library differences, proxies, header limits, backoff/jitter, deadlines, authentication, localization, and sensitive-data review.
